facts.value: 51.02% of borrowing matured under 12 months at 30.9.25, against a 25% upper prudential limit (paper page 9). BREACHED — the only prudential indicator not met in the paper. Disclosed openly with rationale: 'Due to the strategy of only taking out short term loans the upper limit indicator for the percentage of total loans under 12 months was breached. Once longer-term interest rates reduce the authority will replace short term loans with longer term loans.' Second-largest bucket is 10-years-and-above at 36.74% (limit 100%). facts.value: At 30.9.25 (Table 3, page 4): PWLB £70.10m at weighted 3.45% (WAM 10.63 years); Banks (LOBO) £16.00m at weighted 4.87% (WAM 12.69 years); Local Authorities £41.38m at weighted 4.68% (WAM 0.19 years); Others (fixed term) £0.00m. £16m of LOBO loans at weighted 4.87% (WAM 12.69 years). No banks exercised their option during the first six months of 2025/26 (paper page 4 explicit). Paper does not name the lender(s) or call dates.
facts.note: Sector context: across the councils we have read this year, twelve LOBO calls have landed in the same window and every one has been declined by the lender. Stockton's £16m has not been called in H1 2025/26. Modest position; can flag the sector pattern briefly in the email as context for the £16m carrying value.

facts.value: 2.3% (2024/25 actual) rising to 4.6% (2025/26 forecast), then 5.0% in both 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets. Absolute financing costs: £4.3m → £9.0m → £10.1m → £10.4m. The ratio more than doubles between 24/25 actual and 25/26 forecast.

facts.note: The doubling reflects the transition from a lower cost base (mostly historic long-dated PWLB at sub-4%) to significantly more short-dated funding at 4-5% — the same barbell that produced the 51.02% breach. The 'wait for rates to fall' strategy has a visible running cost in the same paper.

The economic data, monetary and fiscal commentary have heightened the downside risks to our Bank Rate forecast, making rate cuts beyond 3.75% increasingly likely.' Inflation printed 3.8% in September, forecast to fall to 3.5% by year end.

source.title: External Context (page 2) and Arlingclose forecast box (page 11)

summary.text:
A 12-page mid-year treasury report to Audit and Governance Committee on 24 November 2025, from Chief Finance Officer Clare Harper. Standalone paper — no appendix; every table sits inside this one PDF. Treasury adviser Arlingclose. Read in full from local PDF.

The one prudential-indicator breach in the paper is deliberate and openly disclosed. At 30 September 2025 51.02% of borrowing sat inside 12 months against a 25% upper limit (page 9). The paper's own words: 'Due to the strategy of only taking out short term loans the upper limit indicator for the percentage of total loans under 12 months was breached. Once longer-term interest rates reduce the authority will replace short term loans with longer term loans.' The book is barbelled — 51.02% under 12m, 0.00% in 12-24m, 10.25% in 24m-5y, just 1.99% in 5-10y, and 36.74% at 10y+. It is a dated, testable strategy in the council's own words.

The rate context has moved against that assumption. At period end (30 September 2025) the 10-year PWLB certainty rate was 5.53% (paper page 4). Today (14 August 2026, notice 314/26 PM) it is 5.83% — +0.30 points on the 10-year since the paper's reference date. The 20-year today at 6.38% is above the paper's period-high of 6.30%. The 50-year today at 6.27% is above the paper's period-high of 6.14%. Bank Rate has fallen once since (4.0% → 3.75%) but the further cuts Arlingclose flagged as 'increasingly likely' in its 10 November 2025 update have not arrived in the eight months since. Meanwhile the same paper shows financing costs as a share of net revenue doubling from 2.3% (24/25 actual) to 4.6% (25/26 forecast), stabilising at 5.0% thereafter (page 11) — the running cost of the wait is visible in the same report.

Borrowing composition at 30.9.25 (Table 3, page 4): PWLB £70.10m at weighted 3.45% (WAM 10.63 years) + Banks LOBO £16.00m at weighted 4.87% (WAM 12.69 years) + Local Authorities £41.38m at weighted 4.68% (WAM 0.19 years) = £127.48m at blended 4.00% (WAM 8.02 years). LOBO position modest with no calls exercised in H1. LA short-term book at 0.19-year WAM = ~70 days: this is the rolling short-end book that is driving the 51.02% breach.

Balance-sheet identity closes on the paper's own convention. Strict CIPFA at 31.3.25: £195.86m CFR - £150.78m external - £9.15m other debt liabilities = £35.93m internal borrowing. The paper's Liability Benchmark table (page 8) prints £45.1m for the same date — that equals £195.86m - £150.78m without netting off the £9.15m of PFI/leases. Difference between the two conventions = £9.15m exactly. Both self-consistent; noted internally.

Loan-book reconciliation with our PWLB file FAILS. Paper Table 3 at 30.9.25 shows PWLB £70.10m at weighted 3.45%; our file returns 42 loans totalling £108,687,365 at 3.8392%, with £84,956,828 outstanding on the live subset at 2026-08-16. Both our figures are higher than the paper's PWLB figure. Same shape as the Slough / Leicester / Redcar reconciliation failures — the file anchors to newer drawdown metadata. Per PIPELINE.md kept out of the email entirely, no quote of our figure, no quote of theirs as if we had checked it, no invitation to correct. Break-cost figures from price_book (£78.2m indicative settlement on £85.0m balance, net £6.76m discount = 8.0% of principal, 28 loans below par, 13 above) held internally for the same reason — sit on a book that does not tie.

The lead for the email is the moved market against the paper's own dated strategy. Secondary: the LOBO cross-council pattern (twelve calls landed, twelve declined) as context for Stockton's £16m holding. The pooled-property-fund statutory-override sunset in April 2029 (page 6) sits alongside a £1.962m reserve — a fair third if space allows.

PWLB strategy in a rising-rate window
officer.body:
Dear Clare,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy Mid Year Report you took to Audit and Governance on 24 November 2025, ahead of the mid-year 2026/27 report that would fall around the same time this year. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper is unusually candid about the one indicator you breached and why, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The first thing that struck us is that your maturity-structure explanation on page 9 is a dated, testable statement of position, which most papers are not: 51.02% under 12 months against a 25% upper limit, breached deliberately because the plan is to replace short-term loans with longer-term ones 'once longer-term interest rates reduce'. That's an admirably clean framing. What we can add from outside is where that curve has gone since your 30 September reference date. Your paper quotes PWLB 10-year certainty ending the half at 5.53%. On the notice today it's 5.83%, so about 0.30 points higher than your period-end. Your 20-year range in the paper was 5.71% to 6.30%; today's 6.38% sits above the top of that range. The 50-year was 5.46% to 6.14% in the period; today it's 6.27%, also above the paper's high. Bank Rate has come off once since (from 4.0% to your Arlingclose central case of 3.75%) but the further cuts Arlingclose flagged as 'increasingly likely' in its 10 November update haven't landed in the eight months since. The full curve and SONIA path are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

What makes that context material for Stockton rather than generic is what sits alongside on your page 11. Your financing costs as a share of net revenue go from 2.3% in the 2024/25 actual to 4.6% in the 2025/26 forecast, and settle at 5.0% in 26/27 and 27/28 — the running cost of the barbell is already in the same paper. Since your Liability Benchmark on page 8 has £97.1m of new borrowing by 31 March 2027 and £100.1m by 31 March 2028, that's a lot queued behind a rate view that has moved further from the trigger in the year since. Nothing follows from us as advice — we don't sell treasury products and every council's cashflow and refinancing shape is its own — but the shape of the trade-off is exactly what pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is built to show against the day's fixings.

One piece of sector context on your LOBO position because it's something no single council can see. Your Table 3 carries £16m of LOBO at weighted 4.87% with 12.69 years' WAM, and page 4 confirms no lender exercised the option in the first half. Across the councils we've read this year twelve LOBO calls have landed in the same window, and every one of them has been declined by the lender — Dexia's calls at Kent and Tameside, three rejected calls at Wolverhampton, one at Staffordshire, KBC's two loans at Bath & NE Somerset going floating with six-monthly resets rather than a rate rise, among others. Twelve for twelve, no cases the other way. That's context for the £16m you carry rather than a call to do anything with it.

Where you might find us most useful for the day-to-day is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, which prices every published council's PWLB book against the DMO's premature-repayment curve. One caveat we owe you before you look: our PWLB file for Stockton has a coverage gap on some of the pre-existing long-dated tail, so we're flagging that rather than presenting our numbers as your position — the same shape we've seen at Slough, Leicester and Redcar, where the file anchors to newer drawdown metadata. Anything drawn during the strategy period, and the monthly sector totals at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, we can benchmark with confidence.

Standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark work is becoming central to how the whole strategy is framed. Your Table on page 8 already shows the shape — declining external borrowing meeting a rising Liability Benchmark of £157.4m by 31 March 2028 — and an interactive version tied to our live rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. For a strategy staged around when to term out, being able to move the reserves path and the assumed new-borrowing rate and see the crossover shift is the useful thing.

On training, five look most relevant to Stockton. Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members) is written for the Audit and Governance Committee members this report goes to. PWLB strategy in a rising-rate window fits the barbell your Table 3 sets out. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets speaks to the £41.38m of LA short-term you carry at 0.19-year WAM. Liability benchmark modelling for treasury goes to your page 8. LOBO loans (legacy) covers the mechanics of what happens when a call date does land, which sits behind the sector pattern above. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
